events.title: AWS Student Builder Group UCC Launch: Your Cloud Journey Starts Here
events.summary: The online launch of the group: who we are, the basics of cloud computing, and advice on getting started from guest speaker Isaac Tandoh.

review.notes: No end time in any source. endsAt equals startsAt, so the site shows the start time only. Body follows the recap (S6); the announced live Q&A is not claimed.

events.body:
## Day One

We launched the AWS Student Builder Group at University of Cape Coast on Google Meet, for students interested in cloud computing, AWS, DevOps and technology more widely. It was free, and no AWS experience was needed.

We introduced the group, explained why we were starting it and what students could expect, and shared the activities we had planned. Then we went through the fundamentals of cloud computing.

## Guest speaker

Isaac Tandoh, AWS Cloud Trainer and DevOps Engineer, talked about how cloud and AWS are used in industry, where DevOps fits, and how students can start learning. Matthew Ntsiful also joined us and shared some of his own experience and encouragement.

Our recap ended: "Day One is officially in the books. Now, we build!"

events.body:
## About the session

Our second event focused on turning an interest in cloud computing into a practical plan. We walked through the AWS certification pathway, from Foundational to Associate, Professional and Specialty, and discussed cloud roles open to students at different stages.

## Guest speaker

Nathaniel Agbenyenu: Senior DevOps Engineer, Cloud Security and FinOps Lead at IT Consortium, and Co-Lead of AWS User Group Accra.

## What we talked about

- AWS certifications and where they fit
- Career paths in cloud computing
- The skills that matter beyond certifications
- Opportunities for students who want to work in cloud

The point that stood out: certifications can be part of the path, but they are not the goal. Practical skills, experience and steady learning matter just as much. Nathaniel closed with a simple reminder: "We don't give up over here."

events.body:
## About the session

From Code to Cloud was our first in-person build session, in the Computer Lab at the New Science Annex. The goal was to take a personal portfolio from a local folder to a live website on AWS, then connect it to an Amazon EC2 backend. We got into the lab half an hour late, at 10:00 AM, so we finished at 2:00 PM instead of 1:00 PM.

## What we did

- Joel Anarba Amuni, our group leader, introduced the group, and attendees signed up to AWS Builder Center with the group's invite link.
- Joel then covered what cloud computing and AWS are, the Europe (Ireland) Region, the two services for the day, Amazon S3 and Amazon EC2, and AWS account safety basics.
- Lab 1, led by Kelvin Opoku Boateng: participants added their own name, bio and projects to the starter portfolio, created an S3 bucket, uploaded the files, enabled static website hosting and opened their live link.
- Then we broke the sites on purpose. Kelvin triggered an Access Denied error, and the room read the error and fixed the bucket policy.
- Lab 2: participants launched an Amazon EC2 instance from a startup script, added its address to the site's config.js and re-uploaded it, so the visit counter and guestbook on their portfolio ran from their own server.
- A 20-question Wayground quiz over refreshments. The top three won group swag, to be handed over when it arrives.
- A group photo, and a reminder to terminate the EC2 instances so they stop running. The websites stay live.

posts.title: Our first website on Amazon S3
posts.excerpt: Week 3 of the Zero to Cloud Practitioner bootcamp took participants from understanding compute and storage concepts to deploying a working Hostel Finder website on Amazon S3. There were new AWS concepts to explore, configurations to work through, and a practical lesson in learning by doing.
posts.author: AWS Student Builder Group at UCC

review.notes: Expanded from detailed community notes supplied by Joel (24 Nov 2026) and sources S1, S2 and S13. Session date Sat 31 Oct 2026 is derived from the post timestamp and photo filenames.

posts.body:
## From concepts to a working website

The third week of our Zero to Cloud Practitioner bootcamp was an opportunity to put some of the concepts participants had been learning into practice.

We began with two important areas of cloud computing: compute and storage. Using real-life examples, we explored what these concepts mean, the roles they play in everyday applications, and how they fit into the infrastructure behind the digital services we use.

Understanding these concepts is an important part of learning AWS. Applications need computing resources to run, while their files and other data need somewhere to be stored and accessed. Knowing how these pieces fit together helps make the different AWS services easier to understand.

After working through the concepts, we moved into the practical session. Participants were guided through deploying a Hostel Finder website using Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).

The objective was to take a website and make it accessible over the internet using an AWS storage service. By the end of the exercise, every participant had successfully deployed the website and made it publicly accessible.

For many participants, this was an important step in connecting what they had been learning about cloud services with something they could actually deploy and access.

## Learning through the errors

Getting the website deployed was not entirely straightforward.

Some participants encountered difficulties with configurations and bucket policies during the process. These challenges required troubleshooting, careful attention to settings, and guidance from others as participants worked towards getting their websites online.

That was an important part of the exercise. Working with cloud services involves more than following instructions and expecting everything to work on the first attempt. Understanding configurations, recognising errors, and knowing how to investigate and resolve them are all part of developing practical cloud skills.

Participants worked through the issues with collaborative guidance, helping one another understand what was going wrong and how to move forward.

Eventually, everyone reached the same goal: a working Hostel Finder website deployed on Amazon S3.

## A podium to finish

After the practical session, we wrapped up the day with a Kahoot quiz covering topics from the first three weeks of the bootcamp.

It was a chance for participants to revisit what they had learned, test their understanding, and bring some friendly competition into the session.

Congratulations to everyone who made it onto the podium and took home some AWS swag. It was a good way to close a session that had combined new concepts, hands-on practice, troubleshooting, and a little competition.

## Next: Exploring more compute services

The following Saturday was set to take participants further into AWS compute services, with practical introductions to Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Lambda.

Having explored storage and deployed a website using Amazon S3, the next step was to understand other ways applications can run on AWS, including virtual computing resources and serverless computing.

The bootcamp continues to build on each session, helping participants develop their understanding of cloud computing while gaining practical experience with AWS services.

**From learning the concepts to deploying a website, Week 3 was another step forward in the journey from zero to cloud.**

posts.title: Certifications are part of the path, not the goal
posts.excerpt: Notes from our second community event, where Nathaniel Agbenyenu shared practical insights on AWS certifications, cloud career paths, and what it takes to build a career beyond passing exams.
posts.author: AWS Student Builder Group at UCC

review.notes: Expanded from detailed community notes supplied by Joel (24 Nov 2026) and sources S4 and S9. No attendance figure stated.

posts.body:
## The conversation

On Saturday, 26 September 2026, we hosted our second official AWS Student Builder Group event, Building Your AWS Career: Certifications, Career Paths & Opportunities, featuring Nathaniel Agbenyenu, Senior DevOps Engineer, Cloud Security and FinOps Lead at IT Consortium, and Co-Lead of AWS User Group Accra.

The session brought together students at different stages of their cloud journey for a conversation about how to move from being interested in cloud computing to building a practical career path in the field.

Nathaniel walked participants through the AWS certification pathway, covering the different levels from Foundational to Associate, Professional, and Specialty certifications. He also shared insights from his professional experience, helping students understand the kinds of career opportunities available in cloud computing and the skills that employers look for beyond formal qualifications.

The discussion also highlighted learning resources and opportunities that students can take advantage of as they develop their knowledge of AWS and prepare for careers in the cloud ecosystem. We concluded with a live question-and-answer session, giving participants the opportunity to ask questions and engage directly with someone working in the industry.

## The point that stuck

One of the strongest takeaways from the session was the importance of seeing certifications in the right perspective.

Earning an AWS certification is a valuable achievement. It provides a structured way to learn cloud concepts, demonstrates an understanding of particular services, and can help establish a foundation for further professional development. But passing an exam alone does not make someone ready to work in the industry.

Practical experience, the ability to solve problems, and a willingness to keep learning are equally important. Students need to go beyond studying for exams by experimenting with AWS services, working on projects, understanding how systems operate, and developing the confidence to apply what they have learned.

That distinction shaped the conversation. Rather than treating certification as the final destination, we were encouraged to approach it as one part of a much longer learning and professional development journey.

## The closing line

As the session came to a close, Nathaniel left us with a simple reminder that captured the spirit of the discussion:

> "We don't give up over here."

It was a fitting way to end an evening centred on learning, career growth, and the work required to build a place for yourself in the technology industry. Progress in cloud computing takes consistency. There will be new concepts to understand, unfamiliar tools to work with, and challenges that require patience. What matters is staying committed to the process and continuing to put what you learn into practice.

We are grateful to Nathaniel for sharing his experience, answering questions, and giving our community a more practical perspective on the opportunities ahead.

## Taking the next step

For many students, understanding the different AWS certification paths and the career opportunities available is an important first step. But knowing where to begin is only part of the journey. The real progress comes from taking that knowledge further, exploring the technology, working on practical projects, and developing skills through consistent practice.

That is the kind of learning environment we want to encourage at AWS SBG UCC. Through conversations with people working in the industry, technical sessions, hands-on workshops, and shared learning experiences, we hope to help students make more informed decisions about their career paths and find opportunities to put their knowledge into practice.

Thank you to Nathaniel Agbenyenu for sharing his time and experience with our community, and to everyone who joined the session and contributed to the conversation.

This is one step in our journey of learning, building, and growing together.

posts.title: The day AWS SBG UCC began
posts.excerpt: On 22 August 2026, students came together online to launch a community at the University of Cape Coast, built around a shared opportunity to explore cloud technology, learn from industry experience, and discover what they can build together.
posts.author: AWS Student Builder Group at UCC

review.notes: Expanded from detailed community notes supplied by Joel (24 Nov 2026) and sources S6, S7, S8 and S11. No attendance figure or end time stated.

posts.body:
## Our first gathering

On Saturday, 22 August 2026, we officially launched the AWS Student Builder Group at the University of Cape Coast (AWS SBG UCC) through an online meeting on Google Meet.

The launch brought together students interested in cloud computing, AWS, DevOps, and the wider world of technology. For some, it was an opportunity to explore cloud computing for the first time. For others, it was a chance to connect with people who shared similar interests and learn about the opportunities ahead.

We began by introducing AWS SBG UCC, the people behind the initiative, and what members could expect from the community. We shared our plans to create opportunities for students to learn, gain practical experience, work on projects, and connect with others who are interested in building with technology.

An important part of this introduction was explaining who the community is for. Cloud computing is often associated with Computer Science, Information Technology, and software engineering, but its applications extend far beyond those disciplines. Students do not have to be studying Computer Science or have a technical background to begin understanding the cloud.

Cloud technology supports services and solutions across finance, healthcare, education, agriculture, research, business, entertainment, and many other areas. It provides the infrastructure behind applications, data platforms, digital services, and systems that people and organisations rely on every day. As more industries adopt digital technologies, understanding how the cloud works becomes increasingly relevant to people working in different fields.

We want students from across UCC to be able to recognise those connections and explore how cloud technology relates to their own academic interests and future careers. Whether someone wants to build software, analyse data, improve a business process, support research, or explore technology in another discipline, there is room to learn and discover something valuable.

## Understanding cloud computing

Following the introduction to the community and its core team, our Technical Lead took participants through the fundamentals of cloud computing.

The aim was to establish a shared understanding of what cloud computing means, how it works, and why it has become an important part of modern technology. Rather than assuming everyone already understood the subject, this session provided a starting point for members who were new to the concept.

Understanding these fundamentals matters because cloud computing is much more than knowing how to use a particular AWS service. It involves understanding how computing resources, storage, databases, networking, and other services can be accessed and used to build and support applications and systems.

For students beginning their journey, having this foundation makes it easier to understand the technologies they will encounter as they progress into practical learning.

## Learning from people in the field

One of the highlights of the launch was our session on **Cloud and AWS in the Real World and Starting Your Cloud Journey**, led by our guest speaker, Isaac Tandoh, an AWS Cloud Trainer and DevOps Engineer.

The session was an opportunity to connect the concepts introduced earlier with how cloud technology is used in professional environments. Beyond understanding what cloud computing is, students needed to see why it matters, the kinds of problems it helps solve, and how they could begin developing skills in this area.

Isaac shared practical insights from his experience in cloud and DevOps, helping participants understand the possibilities available to people who choose to explore this field. His contribution also gave students a clearer perspective on taking their first steps, learning the relevant technologies, and working towards opportunities in the cloud ecosystem.

We also had Matthew Ntsiful join the conversation and share some of his experience and encouragement with the community. Hearing from people with experience in the field was an important part of the launch because students benefit from understanding not only the technologies themselves, but also the different paths people take to learn, develop, and work with them.

The session was followed by a question-and-answer segment, where participants had the opportunity to engage with the speakers, seek clarification, and raise questions about cloud computing and getting started.

We are grateful to Isaac Tandoh and Matthew Ntsiful for giving their time, sharing their experiences, and helping make our first gathering a meaningful learning experience.

## Building a community where everyone can grow

The launch was not just about introducing AWS or explaining cloud computing. It was also about sharing the kind of learning environment we want AWS SBG UCC to become.

We believe students should have opportunities to explore technologies beyond what they encounter in their individual programmes of study. A student studying business should be able to understand how cloud platforms support modern businesses. Someone interested in agriculture should be able to explore how cloud infrastructure can support data collection, analysis, and digital agricultural solutions. Students interested in health, education, engineering, research, and other disciplines should also be able to discover where these technologies fit into their fields.

This does not mean everyone has to become a cloud engineer or pursue the same career. It means having the opportunity to understand the technology, identify where it is useful, and develop skills that complement one's own interests and ambitions.

We want to create an environment where beginners feel comfortable asking questions, experienced students can share what they know, and members can learn from one another. A place where people can exchange ideas, collaborate across disciplines, experiment with AWS services, work on practical projects, and develop the confidence to turn what they learn into something useful.

Through technical sessions, workshops, hands-on projects, certification preparation, industry conversations, and collaborative learning, we hope to make learning more accessible and practical for students at UCC.

There is no expectation that someone must already understand cloud computing before joining. Everyone starts somewhere, and we want the community to make that first step easier.

## What comes next

During the closing segment, we shared what members could look forward to and how they could remain involved in the community.

The launch was the starting point for a longer journey. We want to build on the interest generated during that first gathering by creating consistent opportunities for students to learn, practise, connect, and build together.

Our plans include practical learning experiences, technical workshops, certification preparation, projects, and opportunities to engage with people who have experience in the industry. More importantly, we want these activities to help members move from simply hearing about cloud technology to understanding it, using it, and exploring what they can do with it.

To everyone who attended, participated, supported the announcement, or contributed behind the scenes, thank you for helping us make our first gathering possible. We are especially grateful to our speakers and the core team for their contributions.

AWS SBG UCC is being built for students who are curious about technology and willing to learn, regardless of their starting point or academic background. If you are interested in cloud computing, AWS, software development, DevOps, or discovering how technology connects to your field, there is a place for you in this community.

**We started with a conversation. Now, we look forward to learning, building, and growing together.**

Connect with AWS SBG UCC on [Meetup](https://www.meetup.com/aws-sbg-at-university-of-cape-coast), [WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/BnlWXQsAiJxBmZJwyYnpu0), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/awssbgucc), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/awssbgucc), and [X](https://x.com/awssbgucc), or [reach out on our contact page](/contact).
